interest: This file offers a revealing glimpse into the growing economic, geopolitical, and agricultural anxieties in New Zealand and Australia regarding Imperial Japan during the interwar period. It documents Japan's efforts to achieve raw-material self-sufficiency in fiber and cordage production by importing and acclimatizing Phormium tenax (New Zealand flax), threatening New Zealand's export market. It also reflects how U.S. consular officials monitored Japanese commercial expansion and dominion trade protectionism across the South Pacific in the early 1930s.
overview: This file (894.61323/1) relates to Japanese efforts in 1934 to establish a domestic flax-growing industry by importing Phormium tenax (New Zealand flax) plants. The file consists of a State Department Document File Note cross-referencing Wellington Periodic Report No. 25 (847h.00 P.R./25), dated February 2, 1934, along with the excerpted two-page section of that report prepared by the American Consulate General in Wellington, New Zealand. The report details local press commentary surrounding an initial Japanese order of 40,000 flax plants (with prospects for another 100,000), noting widespread concern in New Zealand and Australia over Japanese commercial penetration, potential competition in global cordage markets, and the wisdom of providing planting stock to a rival nation.

subfiles.about: Consular report excerpt detailing New Zealand press reaction and public apprehension regarding Japanese procurement of New Zealand flax plants for domestic cultivation.
subfiles.summary: An excerpt (pages 11–12) from Wellington Periodic Report No. 25 discussing Phormium tenax (New Zealand flax), a native plant used in manufacturing cordage and sacks. The report describes prominent New Zealand press attention regarding a Japanese order for 40,000 plants, with potential subsequent orders of 100,000 plants if successful. It highlights growing concern in New Zealand and Australia over Japan's expanding sphere of operations and the economic threat of Japan cultivating the crop to compete in global export markets.
